I coach finance people for a living and I hear the same thing every week. Somebody asks a simple question and the answer starts in nineteen ninety eight. The reasoning is understandable. You want to give context so the conclusion makes sense, and in a written report that is exactly right. In a room it is fatal, because the listener does not know where you are going, so they cannot tell which parts matter, so they stop tracking and start waiting. And once somebody is waiting, you have lost them, and nothing you say for the next ninety seconds will land. So here is the rule I give everybody and nobody likes at first. Say the conclusion in one sentence, then say how many reasons there are, then give them. Headline, signpost, detail. If you are wrong about the conclusion, they will interrupt you in fifteen seconds instead of two minutes, and honestly that is a gift.

The short answer is that we protected the margin and lost about a fifth of the revenue, and I would make the same decision again. There are three reasons. The first is that the client was structurally unprofitable and everybody in the room knew it, so keeping it would have meant funding it out of the other accounts. The second is timing. We had six weeks of visibility before the renewal, which was enough to rebuild the cost base but not enough to replace the volume, so the sequence had to be cost first. And the third, which is the one people forget, is that the team needed to see us make an unpopular decision on purpose rather than have it made for us. What I would underscore is the sequence. It was not the cut that saved the margin. It was doing it in that order.
